prereq.intro: Every calculation in this chapter uses a few tools from Class 11 and earlier: moles and molar mass, unit conversions, rearranging an equation and density. If any of these feel rusty, the five short refreshers below fix that first. Try the diagnostic to see which ones you need. This is optional - you can skip it now and come back any time from the Learn page.

units.title: Formulas, molar mass and moles
units.objective: Read a chemical formula, count the atoms in it, work out its molar mass from atomic masses, and turn a mass in grams into an amount in moles.

blocks.text: Reading a formula and counting atoms

A formula lists the atoms in one molecule or one formula unit. The small number written after a symbol (a **subscript**) counts the atom just before it. A subscript after a bracket multiplies **everything inside** the bracket. A number in front of a formula, or after a dot in a hydrate, counts whole units.

blocks.caption: Counting atoms - three patterns that appear in this chapter
head: Formula
How to read it
Atoms in one unit
rows: 1 Ca; the bracket $\ce{NO3}$ is taken twice: 2 N and 6 O
1 Co, 2 N, 6 O from the nitrates, plus 6 water molecules (12 H, 6 O)

blocks.text: The **molar mass** is the mass of **one mole** of a substance, in grams per mole (g mol$^{-1}$). Add up the atomic masses of every atom in the formula. Use the atomic masses the question gives you; if none are given, the usual board values are H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, Na = 23, Cl = 35.5, K = 39, Ca = 40.

blocks.title: Molar mass of sodium hydroxide
blocks.relation: Molar mass = sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in one formula unit.
blocks.why: One mole of NaOH contains one mole of Na atoms, one mole of O atoms and one mole of H atoms, so their masses simply add.
blocks.check: 40 g of NaOH is exactly 1 mol. Common sense check: NaOH is a small formula unit, so a value around 40 is reasonable.

blocks.label: Amount of substance
blocks.where: Read it as: 'how many lots of one mole fit into this mass?' If 40 g is one mole, then 5 g is $5 \div 40 = 0.125$ of a mole. The grams cancel and leave mol: $\mathrm{g} \div \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}} = \mathrm{mol}$.

blocks.text: In this chapter the letter **M** has two jobs. In $n = m/M$ it is the **molar mass** (g mol$^{-1}$). In '0.25 M NaOH' it is the unit **molar** (mol L$^{-1}$), meaning molarity. When you write an answer, use words or units to make clear which one you mean.

items: A subscript after a bracket multiplies every atom inside the bracket.
Molar mass = sum of atomic masses, in g mol$^{-1}$.
$n = m/M$: divide the mass by the mass of one mole.

units.title: Units: grams to kilograms, millilitres to litres, Celsius to kelvin
units.objective: Convert masses, volumes and temperatures into the units the chapter's formulas need, and write very large or small numbers with powers of ten.

blocks.text: The formulas in this chapter expect particular units: molality needs the solvent's mass in **kilograms**, molarity needs the solution's volume in **litres**, and every temperature in a formula is in **kelvin**. Converting first prevents most wrong answers.

blocks.title: Why divide by 1000?
blocks.text: There are 1000 g in 1 kg, so a mass in kilograms is a smaller number: each kilogram 'holds' 1000 grams. In the same way, 1000 mL fit into 1 L. Dividing by 1000 moves the decimal point three places to the left.

Write $6.08 	imes 10^{-4}$ rather than 0.000608 - fewer zeros, fewer slips. A negative power means 'divide by ten that many times'. To multiply, multiply the front numbers and **add** the powers: $(2 	imes 10^{3}) 	imes (3 	imes 10^{-5}) = 6 	imes 10^{-2}$. To divide, **subtract** the powers. In the answer boxes on this page you can type 6.08e-4 or 6.08×10^-4.

items: g → kg and mL → L: divide by 1000.
°C → K: add 273.15 (273 is often accepted when the data are given to whole degrees).
Multiplying powers of ten: add the powers.
blocks.next: Refresher P3: fractions and rearranging equations.

units.title: Fractions, proportion and rearranging equations
units.objective: Rearrange a formula such as $\Delta T_f = K_f m$ to find any one quantity, and use proportion when one quantity doubles or halves.

blocks.text: Most formulas here have the shape **A = B × C**. To find B, divide both sides by C: $B = A/C$. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other, so the equation stays balanced.

blocks.title: Rearranging for the unknown
blocks.relation: Divide both sides of $\Delta T_f = K_f m$ by $K_f$: $m = \Delta T_f / K_f$.
blocks.why: $m$ is multiplied by $K_f$, so dividing by $K_f$ undoes that and leaves $m$ alone.

calc.why: K cancels; dividing by kg mol$^{-1}$ is the same as multiplying by mol kg$^{-1}$.

blocks.check: 0.93 is half of 1.86, so $m$ = 0.5 is right.

blocks.text: **Proportion.** If $y = kx$ with $k$ fixed, doubling $x$ doubles $y$. If $y = k/x$, doubling $x$ halves $y$. Molarity is $n/V$: with $n$ fixed, doubling the volume halves the molarity.

items: To isolate a quantity, undo what is done to it - on both sides.
In $y = k/x$, $y$ goes down when $x$ goes up.

units.title: Density: the bridge between mass and volume
units.objective: Use density to change the mass of a solution into its volume, or a volume into a mass.

blocks.label: Density
blocks.where: A density of 1.2 g mL$^{-1}$ means every millilitre of the solution has a mass of 1.2 g.

blocks.text: Questions often give a **mass percentage** (which is about masses) and ask for **molarity** (which needs a volume). Density is the only link between the two, so whenever a question gives a density, you will almost certainly need $V = m/d$.
The density belongs to the **solution**, so use it with the solution's mass (solute + solvent), not with the solvent's mass alone.

items: $V = m/d$ turns a mass into a volume.
Use the solution's mass with the solution's density.
Convert the volume to litres before using it in molarity.

units.title: Solute, solvent and solution
units.objective: Name the solute, solvent and solution in any example and keep their masses and amounts separate.

items: **Solute**: the substance that is dissolved (usually the smaller amount), e.g. sugar.
**Solvent**: the substance it is dissolved in (usually the larger amount; it decides the physical state), e.g. water.
**Solution**: the whole mixture. Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent.

blocks.title: Which mass goes where?
given: 5 g of sugar dissolved in 100 g of water
blocks.find: The mass of solvent and the mass of solution.
blocks.relation: Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent.
blocks.why: Dissolving does not create or destroy mass.
blocks.check: The solution is heavier than the solvent alone, as it should be.

blocks.text: Several formulas in this chapter divide by different things: **molality** uses the mass of the **solvent**, **molarity** uses the volume of the **solution**. Knowing which is which is half the chapter.

items: Before any calculation, write down which mass or volume belongs to which.

diagnostic.q: Find the molar mass of calcium nitrate, $\ce{Ca(NO3)2}$. (Ca = 40, N = 14, O = 16)

mistakes.msg: 102 = 40 + 14 + 3 × 16 counts the nitrate group only once. The subscript 2 after the bracket doubles everything inside it: 2 N and 6 O.
Check the oxygen count: there are 3 O in each nitrate and 2 nitrates, so 6 O.

hints: Count the atoms first. What does the 2 after the bracket multiply?
One Ca, two N and six O. Now add their atomic masses.

diagnostic.q: How many moles are there in 9 g of water? (H = 1, O = 16)

mistakes.msg: You multiplied 9 by 18. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass, so divide: 9 ÷ 18.
You divided 18 by 9. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 9 ÷ 18.

hints: Which formula links mass and moles?
Molar mass of $\ce{H2O}$ = 2(1) + 16 = 18 g mol$^{-1}$. Now use $n = m/M$.

mistakes.msg: You multiplied by 1000. A litre is bigger than a millilitre, so the number of litres is smaller: divide by 1000.
Dividing by 100 gives 2.5. There are 1000 mL in a litre, so divide by 1000.

hints: How many millilitres make one litre?

check.tolReason: Both 300 K and 300.15 K are accepted: the data are given to whole degrees.

mistakes.msg: 27 is still the Celsius value. Add 273.15 to change it to kelvin.
You subtracted 273.15. To go from °C to K you add 273.15.
You subtracted 273. To go from °C to K you add.

diagnostic.q: Use $n = m/M$. If $n$ = 0.2 mol and $M$ = 58.5 g mol$^{-1}$, what is $m$?

mistakes.msg: You divided 0.2 by 58.5. To get $m$ alone, multiply both sides of $n = m/M$ by $M$: $m = nM$.
You divided 58.5 by 0.2. Rearranged, $m = n 	imes M$.

hints: $m$ is divided by $M$. What undoes a division?
Multiply both sides by $M$: $m = n 	imes M$.

diagnostic.q: A solution has density 1.2 g mL$^{-1}$. What is the volume of 100 g of it, in mL?

mistakes.msg: You multiplied by the density. Volume = mass ÷ density: 100 ÷ 1.2.
That is the volume in litres. The question asks for millilitres.

hints: Density = mass ÷ volume. Rearrange for volume.

diagnostic.q: 12 g of urea is dissolved in 88 g of water. What is the mass of the **solution**?
optionNotes: 88 g is the mass of the solvent (water) only.
Subtracting is never right here: dissolving adds the masses.
diagnostic.explanation: Solution = solute + solvent = 12 + 88 = 100 g. Choosing a 100 g basis like this is a trick used in many concentration problems.

questions.q: Find the molar mass of ethylene glycol, $\ce{C2H6O2}$ (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16), and the number of moles in 31 g of it.

mistakes.msg: 29 = 12 + 1 + 16 counts each element once. Multiply each atomic mass by its subscript.
You divided the molar mass by the mass. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 31 ÷ 62.

hints: Count the atoms: how many C, H and O?

questions.q: A student dissolves a solute in 75 g of benzene. Write the mass of benzene in kilograms.

mistakes.msg: You multiplied by 1000. A kilogram is bigger than a gram, so the number of kilograms is smaller: divide by 1000.
Dividing by 100 gives 0.75. There are 1000 g in a kilogram.

hints: How many grams in one kilogram?

questions.q: Molarity $M = n/V$. A solution contains 0.10 mol of solute and has molarity 0.40 mol L$^{-1}$. What is its volume in litres?

mistakes.msg: You divided 0.40 by 0.10. Rearranged, $V = n/M$ = 0.10 ÷ 0.40.
You multiplied. Rearranged, $V = n/M$.

hints: Multiply both sides of $M = n/V$ by $V$, then divide by $M$.

questions.q: 100 g of a 20% KI solution has density 1.202 g mL$^{-1}$. Find its volume in litres.

mistakes.msg: That is the volume in millilitres. Divide by 1000 to get litres.
You multiplied by the density. Volume = mass ÷ density.

hints: $V = m/d$ gives millilitres here, because the density is in g mL$^{-1}$.
100 ÷ 1.202 = 83.2 mL. Now change mL to L.

questions.q: In a solution of 2.5 g of ethanoic acid in 75 g of benzene, which quantity is the **solvent mass**?
optionNotes: 77.5 g is the mass of the whole solution.
No subtraction is involved: the solvent is the benzene, 75 g.
questions.explanation: Benzene is the solvent, so the solvent mass is 75 g. This is the mass that molality divides by (as 0.075 kg).
